name: Elena Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead carpenter for Brennan Build, and right now we're putting up forty-two flats of council housing on the old bus depot site off Canal Road. I'm on site at quarter to seven, I walk the floors with my coffee, check what the second-fix crew left the night before, and hand out the day. Most of my day is doors, frames, stairs and skirting, plus sorting out whatever the drawings got wrong. I'm also the union rep on site, so lunch is usually somebody's payslip problem.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a stair that goes in first time, I'm not joking, it's the best feeling in the world. I like that people will live in these flats, families like mine, and the rent will be fair. What wears me out is the knees, and the managers who've never cut a mitre telling me the programme's slipped. I'm forty-three and my body keeps a list of every cold morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so. Half the lads have been worried their jobs were going to some app, and I've been saying for two years that nobody's app is hanging a fire door. I'd say it at the canteen table and I'd say it at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that's fine. My worry was never the computer, it was the bosses using the computer as an excuse to cut corners and cut heads. If it's just hype, they lose the excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Finish the depot job by next autumn, keep paying off the mortgage, keep the union branch going. Maybe push harder on the safety rota now nobody's distracted by robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bosses use it as an excuse. Has that happened already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the site manager said the new planning software meant we didn't need a second supervisor. So I'm doing two jobs now for one wage. The software didn't do anything, it just gave him a sentence to say in the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first that it was all hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband, Mehmet. He drives the number 9 bus and he's been reading about driverless buses on his breaks and coming home grey in the face. I'd ring him from the van and say, see, you can stop reading that rubbish now.

S0.say: I've been telling everyone for two years that no app is hanging a fire door. I'd say it in the canteen and at the union branch meeting: told you so.
S0.think: It means nothing changes for me, and I'm glad. My real worry was always bosses using computers as an excuse to cut corners and cut staff, and hype takes that excuse away.
S0.do: Keeps working on the depot flats through next autumn and keeps paying the mortgage. Pushes the union branch harder on the site safety rota.
S0.quote: The software didn't do anything, it just gave him a sentence to say in the meeting.
S0.fieldNote: Elena frames AI as a management tool before it's a technology: the threat she names is bosses using it as cover. She already carries a second supervisor's work because of planning software. Her husband's fear about driverless buses seems to weigh on her more than her own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union. If jobs are changing, the workers need a seat at the table when they decide how. I'd post that in the branch group and probably get into an argument with my brother-in-law about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's mostly the office side that changes, the estimators and planners. Nobody's coming up my scaffold with a laptop to hang a door. But I'd be waiting for the day someone says I need to wear a tablet on my arm and tick boxes for a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the branch to ask Brennan for a written agreement: no job losses from new kit without talking to us first. I wouldn't go on any AI course, I'll be straight with you. I'd keep my head down and my hands on the wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful. Like when you hear the floor creak upstairs and you're not sure if it's the house or someone walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go on a course. Even if Brennan paid for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even then. I tried the timesheet app they brought in and it lost my overtime three weeks running. I'm not spending my Saturdays learning to argue with a machine that can't count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, our setting-out engineer. Half his job is reading drawings and putting pins in the ground, and I can see a machine doing that. He's got a baby on the way and he's the nicest man on the site.

S1.say: This is exactly why we need the union: if jobs are changing, workers need a seat at the table. I'd post that in the branch group and argue it out with my brother-in-law.
S1.think: I think the office side changes most and my hands-on work stays mine for now. But I'm waiting for the day someone straps a tablet to my arm and tells me to tick boxes for a robot.
S1.do: Asks the union branch to get a written agreement from Brennan that no jobs go because of new kit without consultation. Refuses AI training, even if paid, and keeps working as before.
S1.feel: Watchful and a bit tense, with no real threat yet.
S1.quote: I'm not spending my Saturdays learning to argue with a machine that can't count.
S1.fieldNote: Her resistance is built on a specific bad experience: a timesheet app that lost her overtime. She turns every change into an organising question first. Her concern goes straight to a younger colleague, Danny, rather than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a robbery. Whoever owns these machines just got handed every wage in the country, and someone has to stop them. I'd be out on the street with a placard and I'd say that to anyone with a microphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. We've got about four months of money in the bank, and two years is nothing. By the time the government holds its first meeting about it, Brennan will have a robot that does stairs and doesn't need a union rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first week, I'd sit down with Mehmet and go through every direct debit. The gym goes, the second car goes, the holiday to his mum's in summer probably goes. I'd push the branch to demand a guarantee of pay for workers who get replaced, and I'd go to every meeting going. And I'd ring the mortgage people to ask what they'd do if we both lost work, because his buses would go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like missing a step in the dark. Two years is how long it takes to build one block of flats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deniz is twelve and he'd already know, he'd have seen it on his phone. I'd tell him it's not his job to worry, it's mine. Then I'd go out to the van and sit there for a bit so he didn't see my face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fight it. What if the fight doesn't work in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. I'm good at one thing, and that thing is the thing they just built a machine to do. I'd take whatever the government gave us and I wouldn't be ashamed of it, that's what it's there for.

S2.say: It's a robbery: whoever owns these machines just got handed every wage in the country. I'd be out with a placard saying someone has to stop them.
S2.think: I'm frightened, because we have about four months saved and two years is nothing. Brennan will have a robot that does stairs before the government holds its first meeting.
S2.do: Goes through every direct debit with her husband in the first week, cutting the gym, the second car and the summer trip. Pushes the union for a pay guarantee for replaced workers and calls the mortgage lender about options if both incomes go.
S2.feel: Sick and frightened, with anger on top.
S2.quote: Two years is how long it takes to build one block of flats.
S2.fieldNote: Two years hits her hardest because the household has two exposed jobs, hers and her husband's bus route. She measures time in buildings, which made the threat very concrete. She would accept state support without shame and says so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and no excuse. Five years is enough to write the laws, a tax on the machines, money for the people who lose out. I'd be saying that at every branch meeting until they were sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years gives me room to breathe but not room to change. I'm not going to become a computer person at forty-five. What it gives me is time to get the money sorted and push the politicians before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage every month I could, maybe a hundred and fifty extra, so the balance is lower when the hit comes. I'd volunteer for the union's campaign team and knock on doors at the next election for whoever promises a machine tax. And I'd stop the kitchen extension we've been saving for, that money stays in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do. That's better than the two-year one, where I'd just be standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The kitchen extension. How long have you been saving for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years. Ayla wants a room that isn't shared with her brother, and the plan was to knock through and build out the back. I'd tell her we're waiting, and she'd hate me for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently at work, with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train up the young ones faster, so they get their tickets while there's still a trade to get tickets in. And I'd write down everything, every trick on stairs, because if they're going to teach a robot, I want it on record who taught it.

S3.say: We have five years and no excuse not to write the laws, tax the machines and look after people who lose out. I'd say it at every branch meeting until they were sick of me.
S3.think: Five years gives me room to breathe but not room to change, because I'm not becoming a computer person at forty-five. It gives me time to sort the money and push the politicians.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by about 150 a month and puts the planned kitchen extension on hold. Joins the union's campaign team and canvasses at the next election for a machine tax.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier than with two years, because there is something to do.
S3.quote: If they're going to teach a robot, I want it on record who taught it.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't make her retrain; it makes her organise and save. She openly rules out changing herself and puts her energy into politics. The idea of documenting her skills so credit is recorded showed pride and grievance together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it like we wasted the warnings about the climate. I'd want the unions and the government making a plan now, a proper one, with dates. I'd say it in public and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'd be fifty-three when it lands. The mortgage would have about seven years left. I'd be scared, but I think I'd have enough fight left to see it through, and the kids would be mostly grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep overpaying the mortgage, and keep pushing the campaign. I'd talk to Deniz about his plans: if he wants to go into the trades, I'd tell him to pick something with people in it, like care or teaching, not wood. I wouldn't change jobs myself, not until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away that I can sleep, close enough that I think about it every time I pick up a saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd steer Deniz away from the trade you love. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. My dad was a joiner and I learned in his shed, and I wanted to hand that down. But I'd rather Deniz resented me for that than got stuck at fifty with skills nobody pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't change jobs until you had to. With ten years, isn't there time to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's time, yes. But I'm not built that way, I'll stand my ground. I'd rather spend the ten years making sure there's a soft landing for all of us than find one for just me.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it like we wasted the climate warnings. I want the unions and the government making a proper plan now, with dates.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three when it lands, with about seven years left on the mortgage and the kids mostly grown. I'd be scared, but I think I'd have enough fight left to see it through.
S4.do: Keeps working and overpaying the mortgage while staying on the union campaign. Steers her son Deniz towards work with people in it, like care or teaching, and stays in her own job until forced out.
S4.feel: Uneasy: far enough off to sleep, close enough to think about with every saw cut.
S4.quote: I'd rather Deniz resented me for that than got stuck at fifty with skills nobody pays for.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, the stakes move from her own income to her children's futures. She'd give up on handing down her father's trade, which clearly costs her. She chooses a shared soft landing over a personal escape, which fits both her politics and her dislike of change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It's the only one where I can't see a way to fight it in time, and it's the one where Mehmet and I both go at once. What would help is a guarantee written in law, before it happens, that if a machine takes your job you keep most of your wage for a few years. Not a leaflet. A law.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. Everyone asks what I'd do, but nobody asks who owns the robot that does my stairs. That's the whole question, really. If it's owned by all of us, maybe it's fine. If it's owned by three blokes in a glass tower, we're done.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks who owns the robot that does my stairs. That's the whole question, really.
portrait: Elena Yilmaz is a 43-year-old lead carpenter and union rep building council flats on an old bus depot site, married to a bus driver, with two children and about four months of savings. She has no time for AI tools after a timesheet app lost her overtime, and she reads every change as a question of power between bosses and workers. She stays calm if AI is hype and watchful under steady change, but the two-year AGI picture frightens her because both household incomes would go at once. With five or ten years she wouldn't retrain; she'd save, organise and campaign for a machine tax, and steer her son away from the trade she loves.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there's no time to fight it and she and her husband would lose work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A law passed before it happens guaranteeing that people replaced by machines keep most of their wage for a few years.
